title: Rebuilding test automation and CI/CD after both QA engineers left
question: Tell me about a time you stepped up when your team lost capacity.

situation: When I returned to SWIFT for an instant-payment project, both QA engineers left the team at the same time. We were left with developers but no reliable automated test execution and no centralised environments for running the end-to-end suites.

Without replacing that capability, releases would have depended increasingly on manual testing and individual developer environments, creating both a quality risk and a significant bottleneck for the team.
task: I stepped up to take ownership of the testing infrastructure and rebuild enough of the automation and environment management for the developers to maintain release quality while we waited for new QA engineers to join.
action: I first consolidated the existing Robot Framework tests, which were scattered across several legacy virtual machines, into a single repository. I also refactored the messaging tests so the same framework could exercise exchanges across IBM MQ, ActiveMQ and REST endpoints rather than maintaining separate implementations.

I then automated the test environments with Ansible. I wrote playbooks that provisioned and configured multi-VM environments of up to three nodes running Docker Compose, which made it practical to run operating-system and software-version compatibility matrices automatically.

Finally, I rebuilt the CI/CD layer around Jenkins and CloudBees. I migrated the existing imperative scripts to declarative pipelines and extracted reusable logic into Jenkins shared libraries, making the pipelines easier to maintain and extend.

I also built an SSH remote-testing utility that allowed developers to trigger and debug the automated suites from their own environments rather than having to work directly on the test infrastructure.
result: The team gained an automated end-to-end testing capability without waiting for the QA roles to be filled. Compatibility testing across multi-node environments became repeatable and automated, while the new developer tooling made testing and debugging faster during everyday development.
The infrastructure also gave the incoming QA engineers a much more maintainable foundation to take over rather than requiring them to reconstruct the testing environment from scratch.

challenge: The biggest challenge was working on infrastructure with inherently slow feedback loops. A change to an Ansible playbook or Jenkins pipeline could require a full deployment before I knew whether it worked, so I had to deliberately create faster local feedback and find ways to test the pipeline logic independently.
hardestBug: The biggest technical problem was trying to express increasingly dynamic execution logic directly inside Jenkins declarative pipelines. The declarative syntax became difficult to maintain as the number of execution paths grew. I eventually moved the complex behaviour into reusable Jenkins shared-library functions, leaving the pipeline itself responsible for orchestration rather than implementation.
differently: I would introduce the Jenkins shared-library structure earlier. I initially tried to keep too much of the dynamic behaviour inside the declarative pipelines, which made them harder to reason about and slowed down development. Moving that logic into tested, reusable Groovy code was a much cleaner boundary.
aboutYourself: I learned that I am comfortable stepping outside my normal development responsibilities when the team needs it. I also learned to be more deliberate when working on slow infrastructure problems: when feedback is expensive, investing in small, fast feedback loops is often more valuable than simply iterating faster.
enjoyed: I particularly enjoyed building the SSH remote-testing utility. It started as a small tool to make my own workflow easier, but seeing other developers adopt it and use it to trigger and debug tests made the impact of the work very tangible.
